Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund,
a new wholly owned entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed
$200 million
to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as an LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

items.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
items.content:
Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
Published
Oct 22, 2026
Category
Product
Today, we’re donating
Agent Skills
, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.
Agent interoperability through simplicity
A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.
Donating Agent Skills to AAIF
We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation,
which we co-founded
with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.
We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the
agentskills.io
domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.
Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.
What comes next
We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s
Discord
to give feedback on proposed specification changes.
Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at
agentskills.io
and join the discussion on
GitHub
.

Monthly API credits for Max and Team plans
Updated this week
Copy for LLM
Max and Team plans include monthly credits for the Claude Platform. Use them to build Claude into your own apps and agents with the Claude API. This article explains who's eligible, how to claim your credit, what it covers, and what happens when it runs out.
Available on Max and Team plans, including discounted Team plans. Free, Pro, and Enterprise plans aren't eligible.
Monthly credits by plan
Plan
Monthly credit
Max 5x
$100
Max 20x
$200
Team (Standard seats)
$20 per seat*
Team (Premium seats)
$100 per seat*
Discounted Team plans (Nonprofit, Scientists)
$20 USD per Standard seat and $100 USD per Premium seat*
*On Team plans, credits for all seats are pooled into one monthly balance, capped at $500. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. The pool is calculated from the seats on the plan when the credits are granted.
Eligibility
Active plan.
Your Max or Team subscription must be active and in good standing.
Seven days on the plan.
New subscribers can claim once they've been on an eligible plan for seven days.
Mobile subscriptions.
You can subscribe on the web, iOS, or Android. Claim your credits on claude.ai in a web browser.
No payment method needed.
You don't need to add a card on Claude Platform to claim or use the credit.
How to claim your credit
To claim your credit, you link a Claude Console organization to your plan. Credits go to that organization each month.
Before you begin, you need:
On your Claude plan:
Max: be the subscriber. Team: be a Primary Owner or Owner
In the Console organization:
the Owner, Admin, or Billing role. If you don't have a Console organization yet, you can create one during the claim flow or at
platform.claude.com
.
To claim your credit:
On claude.ai, go to
Settings > Billing
as a Max subscriber or
Organization settings > Billing
as a Team Owner or Primary Owner.
In the
API credits
section, select "Link organization."
Choose the Console organization you want to receive the credits, or create a new one.
Review the
Supplemental Credit Terms
, then Link organization.
Your credits appear in that organization's balance, ready to use.
Important:
You can link only one Console organization, and each Console organization can receive credits from only one plan. You can't change the linked organization yourself, so choose the one you plan to build in. To change it later,
contact support
.
Tip:
Sign in to the Claude Console with the same email you use on claude.ai. If you’re seeing errors during the linking flow, please try again in a few hours.
What the credits cover
The credits work with any available Claude model on the Claude Platform, including:
The Claude API (Messages API and Message Batches API)
The Playground in the Claude Console
Claude Managed Agents
The Claude Agent SDK
The credits don’t apply to:
Interactive Claude Code in the terminal, IDE, desktop, or web
Extra usage in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork
Claude on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry
How the credits work
Refreshes each billing cycle.
New credits arrive shortly after your plan payment goes through. On annual plans, credits arrive monthly.
Doesn't roll over.
Unused credits expire at the end of each billing cycle.
Used first.
Your monthly credits are spent before any credits you've purchased.
Shared across the organization.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization draws from the same balance.
Separate from your plan limits.
The credits don’t change your usage limits in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork.
Visible in the Console.
All credits appear on the
Billing
page (platform.claude.com/settings/billing) in the Claude Console with their amount and expiry date.
What happens when your credits run out
If the organization has purchased credits or auto-reload,
usage continues and draws from those.
If the organization has no other credits,
API requests stop until your next monthly credits arrive. Usage is never charged to your Claude plan. To keep going, buy credits or turn on auto-reload in the Console.
If your organization is invoiced through Anthropic sales,
usage beyond the credits is billed as usual.
If your plan changes
Cancel, downgrade to an ineligible plan, or refund.
New credits stop. Credits you already have stay usable until they expire.
Upgrade from Max 5x to Max 20x.
You receive prorated credits right away, then $200 each billing cycle after that.
Move from Max to Team.
Your Max link ends. A Team Owner or Primary Owner can claim the team's credits once the Team plan has been active for seven days.
For Team Owners and Primary Owners
One claim for the whole team.
One owner links a Console organization and claims the pooled credit, up to $500 a month.
The pool follows your seat count.
It's calculated from the seats on your plan each time credits are deposited. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. Adding another Premium seat would increase the next cycle’s credits to $360.
Control who spends it.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization can use the balance. To limit usage by project or teammate, set
workspace spend limits
in the Console.
Frequently asked questions
Why can't I use the credits for Claude Code?
The credits are for building your own apps and agents on the Claude Platform. They don't cover interactive Claude Code sessions or extra usage after you hit your plan's limits.
Why don't I see the offer yet?
We’re rolling out API credits over a few days so we might not have gotten to you yet. The offer appears after you've been on an eligible plan for seven days. If you're past seven days and still don't see it, check that you're on a Max or Team plan and that you have one of the required roles. If you think you should be eligible but don’t see the API credits,
contact support
.
Is this the same as the Agent SDK credits announced in June?
No. That credit isn't available. API credits cover the Claude API, Claude Managed Agents, and the Claude Agent SDK, and you claim it into a Console organization.
Can I split my credits across multiple organizations?
No. Credits go to a single Console organization.
I'm on a Pro plan. Can I get this credit?
No. The credits are available on Max and Team plans only.
Does this cover
claude -p
?
API credits cover
claude -p
and the Claude Agent SDK when you run them yourself with an API key from your linked Claude Console organization, because that usage is billed as Agent SDK usage. When you're signed in with your Claude plan instead,
claude -p
and Agent SDK usage still draw from your plan's usage limits and don't use your API credits. Runs started by the Claude Code GitHub Action, an IDE extension or the Claude desktop app count as Claude Code usage, so API credits don't cover them, even with
-p
.

Claude Cowork and chat are one Claude
Updated today
Copy for LLM
We’re introducing a new way to use both Claude Cowork and chat that removes the distinction between the two products: in the new experience, these are merged into a single conversation, so you don’t need to decide which option better suits your task before getting started. Ask Claude for what you need, and it can decide which tool to use. Claude can answer a quick question, and it can also take on more complex work, like research, reports, spreadsheets, and presentations, and hand it back as finished files you can edit. With the new Claude experience, you ask for all of it in the same conversation, with no mode to choose. What you could previously only do in Claude Cowork is available from any conversation.
The new Claude experience is rolling out gradually, starting with Pro and Max plans on web, desktop, and mobile. More plans will follow soon, and Enterprise admins will hear from us at least 30 days before anything changes for their organization.
Why you might not have it yet
We're rolling this new experience out in stages, so even accounts on the same plan will see the changes at different times. You don't need to do anything to enable the new experience. If you're on a Pro or Max plan and your message box still shows "Chat" and "Cowork" options, you don't have it yet. Until then, keep using chat and Claude Cowork as you do today, where you can do most of what's in this article. Your chats, tasks, projects, and settings come with you when your account moves over. Once your account has the new experience, you can't switch back to separate "Chat" and "Cowork" options.
What Claude can do
Hand Claude a whole task
Describe the outcome you want, and Claude works through the steps on its own: searching the web, reading your files, running code, and putting the results together. You don't need to break the work into steps or pick a mode first. A quick question still gets a quick answer, and you can have several tasks running at the same time.
Try: "Go through these five interview notes and pull out the top themes, with a quote for each."
Step away while Claude works
More involved tasks keep running in the cloud even if you close your laptop or leave the page. Come back when the task is done, and the result is waiting in the conversation. Tasks that use files or apps on your computer need Claude Desktop open.
Try: "Research the top project management tools for small teams and write up a comparison. I'll check back later."
Get finished files back
Claude can create documents, spreadsheets with working formulas, and presentations you can open in PowerPoint. Download them and use them anywhere, or ask Claude to keep refining them.
Try: "Turn this analysis into a 10-slide deck I can present on Monday."
Create designs, decks, and docs
Claude can build charts, diagrams, and interactive visuals right in the conversation. Learn more in
Custom visuals in chat and Cowork
. On paid plans, you can also ask for a design, deck, or doc for work you'll put in front of others. Claude Design makes on-brand visuals and mockups, Claude Slides makes presentations, and Claude Docs makes living documents you write with Claude and your team (Claude Design, Claude Slides, and Claude Docs are in beta.) Edit the result yourself or tell Claude what to change, then share it by link or export it. Learn more in
What are artifacts and how do I use them?
Try: "Make a one-page visual summary of this launch plan."
Use the apps you've connected
Apps you've connected to Claude (like Google Drive, Gmail, Microsoft 365, or Slack) work while Claude carries out a task, so it can pull what it needs as it goes. Connect apps in
Customize > Connectors
.
Try: "Find last quarter's board deck in my Drive and summarize what changed since."
Work on the web and on your computer
Files and folders:
In Claude Desktop, give Claude access to a folder on your computer so it can read, organize, and create files there.
Browsing:
Claude can open sites, read pages, click, and fill in forms, using the browser built into Claude Desktop or your own Chrome browser through Claude in Chrome. Learn more in
Use the built-in browser in Claude Cowork
.
Computer use:
In beta on Pro and Max plans, Claude can use apps on your computer directly by clicking, typing, and navigating your screen. Learn more in
Let Claude use your computer in Cowork
.
Claude reaches your local files, the built-in browser, and computer use only while Claude Desktop is open, and by default it asks before permanently deleting any files.
Try: "Organize my Downloads folder by file type and date."
Schedule recurring work
Ask Claude to run a task on a schedule, like a summary of your inbox every Monday morning. Scheduled tasks can run in the cloud, so they keep going when your computer is off. Learn more in
Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Cowork
.
Try: "Every weekday at 8 AM, summarize new messages in my team's Slack channels."
Check in from your phone
A task you start at your desk shows up in Claude Mobile too, so you can see how it's going, answer questions from Claude, and redirect the work from anywhere. You can also start a task from your phone, and Claude keeps working in the cloud.
Make Claude your own
Skills:
Teach Claude how you like a task done, and it follows those steps whenever the task comes up. Learn more in
Use skills in Claude
.
Plugins:
Add plugins that bundle skills and connectors for your role. Learn more in
Use plugins in Claude
.
Choose how much Claude checks with you
A permission setting in the message box controls how independently Claude works:
Auto (default on Pro, Max, and Team plans):
Claude keeps working without stopping to ask about each step, and automated safety checks run before it takes an action.
Manual (default on Enterprise plans):
Claude asks before it takes actions, and you choose whether to allow each one.
You can change the setting at any time, and you can stop or redirect Claude while it works. The setting applies to the whole conversation. For work with real consequences, like sending messages or changing important files, stay close and review what Claude does. Learn more in
Use Claude Cowork safely
.
Pick up where you left off
One conversation list:
Your quick questions and longer tasks live together in
Recents
.
Memory:
Claude uses what it remembers from your chats in the tasks it works on for you.
Projects:
Keep files, instructions, and context together for related work. Projects work in every conversation.
Instructions for Claude:
Set preferences that apply to every conversation in
Settings > General
.
What happened to Claude Cowork?
In the new experience, everything Claude Cowork does is available from any conversation. Your existing Cowork tasks, projects, connectors, skills, artifacts, and files carry over, and those Cowork tasks open as they did before, so you can continue them. The model picker and the “Code” tab are where they were.
What's in a new place
Cowork tasks:
Together with your chats in
Recents
.
Global instructions:
The Cowork
Global instructions
setting is now part of
Instructions for Claude
in
Settings > General
. Check that your instructions are what you want.
Web search:
There's no web search toggle. Claude searches the web when it helps.
Research:
Type /deep-research, or click the “+” button below the chat input, then choose “Research.”
Files:
Files Claude creates appear alongside the conversation. In Claude Desktop, the folder Cowork saved its work to is still there. Look for
Storage folder
in
Settings
. Folders you gave Cowork access to are listed under
Trusted folders
.
Memory from local tasks:
Memory from Cowork tasks that ran only on your computer stays with those tasks.
Current limitations
Add from GitHub
isn't supported.
Branching a conversation
from an earlier point isn't available.
Incognito chats
still work, but they open in the previous experience, so Claude can't create files or run code in them.
Search
doesn't include older Cowork tasks. It covers your chats and new conversations, and you can still find older tasks by name in
Recents
.
Dispatch
isn't available to new users. If you already use Dispatch, you can keep using it for now. Learn more in
Assign tasks from anywhere in Claude Cowork
.
How usage works
Everything you do with Claude counts toward your plan's usage limits.  Longer agentic tasks that search the web, run code, or create files generally use more than a quick question. While the new experience rolls out, usage may be measured slightly differently for accounts that have it and accounts that don’t. Check your current usage in
Settings > Usage
, and learn more in
Usage limit best practices

How to Read Data into GPU Memory in Python with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage
Oct 22, 2026
By
Andrew Hoyle
Like
Discuss (0)
L
T
F
R
E
AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA KvikIO
provides high-level Python and C++ interfaces that sit above the cuFile C API to enable accelerated file I/O into GPU memory.
The library and cuFile make independent path-selection decisions: KvikIO chooses whether to invoke cuFile, while cuFile determines whether the transfer uses the accelerated nvidia-fs kernel module or a CPU-staged compatibility path.
Runtime settings such as KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE and KVIKIO_GDS_THRESHOLD control KvikIO's behavior, and cufile.json settings such as execution.parallel_io and execution.min_io_threshold_size_kb shape how cuFile decomposes and schedules requests.
Per-process cuFile statistics collected with CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 and inspected via gds_stats reveal whether operations traveled the nvidia-fs accelerated path (nvfs counters) or the compatibility path (posix counters).
KvikIO is part of the
NVIDIA CUDA-X
libraries for data science and has been used to accelerate I/O in cuDF, cuCIM digital pathology workflows, cuPhoton scientific-image analysis, and GPU-accelerated Presto analytics workloads.
Next Steps
Run the
KvikIO Python example
on a GDS-enabled system to observe the accelerated data path.
Explore the
KvikIO runtime settings
to configure compatibility mode and GDS threshold for specific workloads.
Review the
NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage documentation
for complete installation and platform requirements.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
GPU applications are processing ever-growing datasets with increasingly powerful accelerators. According to the
2025 Stanford AI Index
, compute for notable AI models has been doubling approximately every five months, while the size of datasets used to train LLMs has been doubling approximately every eight months. As computation and data scale together, moving data efficiently from storage becomes a necessity for keeping accelerators supplied.
NVIDIA Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS)
addresses this challenge by enabling a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory. This avoids unnecessary staging through CPU memory and reduces overall CPU utilization in the system. GDS is supported by a growing ecosystem that includes many
major storage vendors
.
At the application layer, Python plays a central role in modern AI development. As of August 2025,
nearly half of all new AI projects on GitHub were built primarily in Python
while the main application interface to GDS is the
cuFile
C API.
NVIDIA KvikIO
, a Python and C++ library for high-performance file I/O, bridges this gap. It provides high-level, idiomatic Python and C++ interfaces, along with additional controls over how I/O requests are performed.
The tutorial in this post demonstrates how to use the NVIDIA KvikIO Python API to configure storage I/O, read data into GPU memory, and confirm that the accelerated path within GDS was activated. It also shows how to inspect the KvikIO and cuFile settings that influence the path each operation takes.
How does NVIDIA KvikIO leverage GDS?
GDS is the broader technology that enables accelerated data movement between supported storage and GPU memory. For file system-based storage, cuFile provides the C library and API through which applications and frameworks access GDS. KvikIO sits above cuFile, providing higher-level Python and C++ interfaces along with its own controls over how I/O requests are executed. Figure 1 shows these layers and their two separate path-selection points. Initialization failures, unsupported configurations, and error-handling paths are omitted for clarity.
Figure 1. Successful execution flow for a KvikIO read
The application supplies a file system path and GPU buffer, and KvikIO determines whether to send the request through cuFile or use its POSIX compatibility path, which stages the data through host memory. When cuFile is selected, KvikIO registers the file and issues the I/O using the target GPU buffer.
cuFile then determines the actual transfer path based on system support, the file system, and its configuration. It may use the accelerated GDS path or its CPU-staged compatibility path. Therefore, reaching the cuFile API confirms that KvikIO selected cuFile, but does not by itself confirm that the accelerated GDS path was activated.
The following sections walk through how to configure the system, perform a KvikIO read, and verify the resulting path.
Prerequisites
Before beginning this tutorial, you will need:
A Linux system with an NVIDIA GPU and GPUDirect Storage installed.
A GDS-supported storage and file system configuration.
Permission to create, read, and write files at the storage endpoint, along with access to GDS tools such as
gdscheck
and
gds_stats
.
For complete installation and platform requirements, refer to the
NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage documentation
.
Tutorial system
This tutorial was tested with the following configuration:
An
x86_64
system with an NVIDIA H100 GPU, CUDA 13.3, and cuFile 1.18.
A local NVMe device formatted with
ext4
.
A PIX connection between the selected GPU and NVMe device, meaning the path traverses at most one PCIe bridge.
IOMMU and ACS disabled to preserve PCIe peer-to-peer transfers.
The
nvidia-fs
kernel module is loaded to provide the accelerated path.
You can inspect the GPU-to-storage topology with the following command:
$ nvidia-smi topo -nvme
Step 1: Set up NVIDIA KvikIO
First, create a Python environment and install the CUDA 13 build of KvikIO. CuPy will be installed as a dependency.
$ python3 -m venv kvikio-env
$ source kvikio-env/bin/activate
$ python -m pip install kvikio-cu13
You can verify the installation with the following:
$ python -m pip show kvikio-cu13 cupy-cuda13x
Step 2: Inspect the configuration
Before performing any I/O, inspect the active KvikIO settings and confirm that the system recognizes the GDS components. In the KvikIO defaults API, the compatibility-mode setting is named
compat_mode
, and its name attribute reports the active mode as
AUTO
,
ON
, or
OFF
. The following commands report the loaded KvikIO and cuFile versions, the active compatibility mode, and the minimum request size KvikIO sends to cuFile:
import kvikio
import kvikio.cufile_driver as cufile_driver
import kvikio.defaults as defaults
kvikio.__version__
cufile_driver.libcufile_version()
defaults.get("compat_mode").name
defaults.get("gds_threshold")
On the tutorial system, KvikIO reports compatibility mode as
AUTO
and a GDS threshold of 16 KiB.
AUTO
instructs KvikIO to try cuFile and fall back to its POSIX backend if cuFile is unavailable. Reads smaller than the threshold use the KvikIO POSIX path directly. These settings can also be controlled through
KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE
and
KVIKIO_GDS_THRESHOLD
. For the complete list, refer to the
KvikIO runtime settings
.
Next, inspect the GDS platform and cuFile configuration:
$ /usr/local/cuda-13.3/gds/tools/gdscheck.py -p 2>&1 | less -R
The output lists the installed GDS components, supported file systems, detected GPUs, and active cuFile configuration. Figure 2 shows how to inspect the KvikIO and GDS configuration used in this tutorial.
Figure 2. A terminal session checking the KvikIO version, cuFile version, compatibility mode, and GDS threshold, then running a GDS diagnostic
KvikIO settings can also be changed in Python. For example,
defaults.set
accepts a dictionary to change several settings at once, or a name and value to change one setting:
defaults.set({"task_size": 1024**3, "num_threads": 8})
defaults.set("compat_mode", kvikio.CompatMode.OFF)
Step 3: Read a file into GPU memory
Next, create the input file once before running the Python example. The following command writes a 1 GiB file with random data using direct I/O and flushes it to storage:
$ dd if=/dev/urandom \
of=/mnt/nvme1/kvikio-tutorial/kvikio-example.bin \
bs=1M count=1024 \
oflag=direct conv=fsync \
status=progress
The following program allocates a 1 GiB CuPy array in GPU memory and supplies it to KvikIO as the destination buffer:
from pathlib import Path
import cupy as cp
import kvikio
file_path = Path(
"/mnt/nvme1/kvikio-tutorial/kvikio-example.bin"
)
# Allocate a GPU buffer large enough to hold the file.
gpu_buffer = cp.empty(
file_path.stat().st_size,
dtype=cp.uint8,
)
# Read the file into the GPU buffer.
with kvikio.CuFile(file_path, "r") as file:
bytes_read = file.read(gpu_buffer)
# Validate that 1 GiB was read.
assert bytes_read == gpu_buffer.nbytes
The context manager opens the file and completes the read into GPU memory. Although the return value confirms that the complete file was read, it does not identify the underlying data path.
Step 4: Determine the data path
One way to validate the data path used by any cuFile-based application is to observe the cuFile runtime per-process statistics. These statistics can be enabled by setting
CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3
and then inspected with
gds_stats
while the process remains active.
For this KvikIO example, the environment variable keeps the setting scoped to a single run, although it can also be configured in
cufile.json
.
$ CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 python3 -i read_with_kvikio.py
Running Python interactively keeps the process alive after the read, allowing
gds_stats
to inspect its accumulated counters.
Figure 3 demonstrates this workflow. In the per-GPU output,
nvfs
counts operations representing the path taken through the
nvidia-fs
kernel module, while
posix
counts operations handled by the cuFile compatibility path.
Figure 3. Terminal session of cuFile statistics for a KvikIO read, showing 256 nvfs reads totaling 1,024 MiB
The KvikIO default 4 MiB task size divides the 1 GiB request into 256 read operations. The per-GPU statistics report
n=256
,
nvfs=256
, and
posix=0
, showing that all 256 operations used the
nvidia-fs
path.
Step 5: Compare the available paths
The same read can be repeated with different settings to demonstrate the two control layers. First, require KvikIO to use cuFile:
$ CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 \
KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE=off \
python3 -i read_with_kvikio.py
On the tutorial system,
gds_stats
reports
nvfs
operations, confirming that cuFile selected the accelerated path. Next, force cuFile to use its compatibility path:
$ CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 \
KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE=off \
CUFILE_FORCE_COMPAT_MODE=true \
python3 -i read_with_kvikio.py
KvikIO still calls cuFile, but the operations now appear under
posix
rather than
nvfs
. Finally, the KvikIO compatibility mode bypasses cuFile entirely:
$ KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE=on \
python3 read_with_kvikio.py
In this case, KvikIO performs the read through its CPU-staged POSIX backend, so cuFile does not record the operation. The next section examines the cuFile settings that control request execution.
Step 6: cuFile configuration for a KvikIO read
After KvikIO selects its cuFile path, cuFile applies another set of controls that determine how the request is executed. These controls are defined in
cufile.json
and operate independently of KvikIO runtime settings.
Request decomposition and parallel execution
KvikIO and cuFile can both divide a large operation into smaller pieces. KvikIO applies
KVIKIO_TASK_SIZE
first, with
KVIKIO_NTHREADS
controlling how those tasks are scheduled. Each task on the cuFile path becomes a separate cuFile request. Once cuFile receives one of those requests, its execution settings determine whether it can be divided again and processed using the cuFile internal thread pool. The following cuFile settings control this behavior:
Setting
Purpose
execution.parallel_io

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA DGX Spark
now supports official eight-node clusters, scaling unified memory to 1 TB and enabling local execution of frontier-class models such as the full GLM 5.3 (753B) from Z.ai.
A Spark-optimized collective backend called RoCEnante reduces all-reduce latency for tensor-parallel decode on switch-connected clusters, delivering a 4.43x decode speedup at eight nodes compared to 3.05x without it.
Benchmark data shows decode throughput scaling from roughly 12 tokens per second on one node to 52 tokens per second on eight nodes using Qwen3.8-27B (NVFP4), with switch topologies enabling flexible workload partitioning and ring topologies offering cost-effective four-node inference.
NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard
routes requests between model pools on a shared eight-node cluster, matching Qwen-only quality on a tool-use benchmark while raising aggregate throughput up to 3x when most traffic shifts to a smaller model.
Pre-training a nanochat model from scratch across eight nodes achieves a 7.79x speedup at 97.4% scaling efficiency, demonstrating near-linear training performance for small models on the desk.
Next Steps
Explore
Connect multiple DGX Spark machines for distributed workloads
to set up a multi-node cluster.
Serve LLMs with
vLLM across DGX Spark
for distributed inference.
Review
model compatibility guide and Switchyard orchestration resources
for multi-model routing.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
AI developers aren’t just running a single model anymore—they’re orchestrating multiple models in parallel, chaining inference calls, and experimenting with frontier-class architectures that demand hundreds of gigabytes of memory.
NVIDIA DGX Spark
was built to bring AI development to the desk, and now you’ll be able to link even more Spark nodes together.
At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA announced official support for eight-node DGX Spark clusters, scaling unified memory to 1 TB and opening the door to frontier-class models, multi-agent workloads, and near-linear pre-training—all running locally.
NVIDIA Sync
makes it easy to cluster. Its Cluster Assistant handles setup and device management. Support for eight-node clusters in NVIDIA Sync is coming by the end of the year.
Read on for benchmark data on how inference, orchestration, and training scale as the cluster grows.
Run larger, newer frontier-class models
The biggest benefit of an eight-node cluster is memory. A single DGX Spark provides 128 GB of unified memory; four nodes reach 512 GB; eight nodes reach 1 TB. That capacity opens the door to a class of models that previously wouldn’t start on a four-node system, including the full GLM 5.3 (753B) model from Z.ai.
Beyond simply fitting these models, the cluster is designed to serve them interactively. As an early example, we ran GLM 5.3 Flash across an eight-node cluster, and measured roughly 80 tokens per second (TPS) in generation, suitable for interactive local development against a frontier-class mixture-of-experts model.
The full GLM 5.3 (753B) checkpoint runs across the 8x 128 GB cluster, making it one of the largest open models you can serve locally.

Table 1. Full GLM 5.3 (nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4) performance on an eight-node DGX Spark cluster. The model is about 470 GB in NVFP4, measured with MTP3 at concurrency one, four, and eight. Prefill measured at 8K input sequence length (ISL) per request.
Faster collectives with a Spark-optimized backend
Tensor-parallel inference spends a meaningful fraction of its time in collective operations such as all-reduce. On switch-connected clusters, we have been evaluating a Spark-optimized collective backend, RoCEnante, that reduces collective latency for the small-message, low-concurrency, modest-rank-count pattern typical of tensor-parallel decode on local AI hardware.
This backend implements an all-to-all exchange followed by local reduction. Each rank shares its input with every other rank, then adds the inputs locally. A single GPU kernel coordinates the exchange and reduction.
The main benefit is fewer communication steps. Ring all-reduce passes data between neighboring ranks over multiple rounds. This approach exchanges data directly with all peers, avoiding that chain of forwarding. For small messages and a modest number of ranks, this can reduce latency.
The tradeoff is more data movement. Each rank sends its full input to every peer and reduces all the inputs itself. As messages or number of ranks (nodes) grow, that extra traffic becomes more expensive, making ring all-reduce’s bandwidth efficiency increasingly attractive. If you need to support high concurrency, larger clusters, or ring topologies, NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) would perform better.
Figure 1. Spark decode scaling with and without ROCEnante on a switch topology using Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 (speculative decoding disabled). At eight Spark nodes, ROCEnante delivers a 4.43x speedup vs. 3.05x without it—a 45% improvement in scaling efficiency.
In practice we see roughly 5% higher prefill and 21% higher decode throughput at four nodes (NVFP4), and about 18% higher decode throughput at eight nodes on the non-quantized model, consistent with the latency-versus-bandwidth tradeoff above. The backend is merged into FlashInfer and falls back transparently to NCCL if its startup test fails.
The backend applies only to switch-connected topologies, because it relies on direct point-to-point exchange between every node. It is not a replacement for NCCL, which remains the supported default and the better choice as cluster size and concurrency grow. The original one-shot all-reduce approach was contributed by the community (Jason Cook/el8).
Two, four, eight: Scaling the cluster
Low-latency NVIDIA
ConnectX-7 NICs
and RDMA on Converged Ethernet (RoCE) communication let DGX Spark nodes exchange tensors efficiently, so you can scale a model across more nodes to fit it in memory and to improve throughput. To isolate cluster scaling behavior and remove context-dependent behavior, we benchmarked a dense Qwen3.8-27B (NVFP4) model without speculative decoding/MTP across one to eight nodes:

Two patterns stand out. First, decode throughput scales strongly with node count, from about 12 TPS on one node to 52 TPS on eight nodes.
Second, the best topology depends on the workload: A physical ring delivers excellent decode throughput for a single model spread across all nodes. A switch is needed once you want to split the cluster into independent groups, or run workloads that require direct any-to-any connectivity between nodes.
To try this yourself,
this networking guide
walks through cluster setup starting from a two-node configuration and scaling up.
Switchless ring topology and setup simplicity
Not every cluster may need a switch. DGX Spark nodes can be wired directly together in a ring, which lowers cost and simplifies setup—an attractive option for enthusiasts and small deployments.
Within a four-node DGX Spark deployment, NCCL defaults to ring-based algorithms for tensor-parallel communication, allowing a switchless ring topology to align perfectly with traffic flows and offer impressive throughput at lower expense. As Table 2 shows, the four-node ring performs well in prefill and decode throughput for this workload.
The picture changes as you scale or specialize:
Eight nodes or split allocations:
If you want to split a cluster into, say, two groups of four, a ring cannot express that topology; you need a switch.
All-to-all and traditional HPC workloads:
Anything that depends on point-to-point patterns (for example, MPI-based clustering) requires a switch; a ring would pay a hop penalty.
The optimized collective backend:
The Spark-optimized backend described above requires direct point-to-point connectivity between every node, so it applies to switched configurations only.
In short: Reach for a switchless ring when you want the simplest, lowest-cost four-node inference box, and choose a switch when you need to scale up to eight nodes, split the cluster, or run communication patterns that a ring cannot serve.
Multi-model orchestration with Switchyard
Not every request needs your largest model. On a shared eight-node cluster, you can get substantially more aggregate throughput by routing easy requests to a small, fast model and reserving a larger model for the hard ones.
NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard
makes this practical: A lightweight classifier inspects each request (or session) and routes it to the appropriate model pool, with a load balancer distributing traffic across replicas. Because this layout splits the eight nodes into independent model pools, Switchyard runs on a switch-connected cluster, which provides the any-to-any connectivity needed to route requests across replicas.
In our prototype, we used OpenBMB’s MiniCPM5 2B as the classifier and execution model for simple tasks and Qwen3.8 Flash Next for complex ones. On a standard-plus-hard tool-use benchmark, the routed agent matched the quality of the Qwen-only configuration while freeing capacity on the cluster.
On the 92-case tool-use benchmark (including hard cases), the routed agent scored 91/100, matching the Qwen-only configuration.
Because MiniCPM serves roughly an order of magnitude more requests per second than Qwen per replica, shifting part of the traffic to the smaller model raises the throughput ceiling of the whole cluster. Allocating three Qwen replicas (two Spark nodes each) and two MiniCPM replicas (one Spark each) across the eight nodes, we get:
~1.5x
aggregate throughput over a Qwen-only baseline when half of requests route to Qwen.
~3.0x
aggregate throughput when a quarter of requests route to Qwen and the rest to MiniCPM.
A routing policy is a simple YAML file, and NVIDIA provides a sample policy as a starting point; developers can tune the split and classifier to their own workload.
Pre-training from scratch: near-linear scaling with nanochat
Training behaves differently from inference. When each node holds a full copy of the model, the only cross-node communication is gradient synchronization once per step, so clustering scales close to linearly. To demonstrate, we pre-trained a nanochat model from scratch (about 896.5M parameters, 20 transformer layers, hidden dimension 1,280- and 2,048-token sequences) and measured training throughput as we added nodes.

Eight nodes deliver a 7.79x speedup at 97.4% efficiency, the kind of near-linear scaling that makes an eight-node Spark cluster a credible platform for training small models from scratch, not just serving large ones. It is also a natural on-ramp workflow: Prototype and pre-train locally, then scale out as the model grows.

Eight-node DGX Spark clusters give you the memory to load frontier-class models, the flexibility to orchestrate several models at once, and the efficiency to train small models from scratch, all on the desk.

items.title: Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud Learn how Project Chrysalis combines Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Agent Development Kit (ADK), Bi
items.content:
Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud
- Google Developers Blog
Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud
OCT. 22, 2026
Anant Nawalgaria
Group Product Manager & AI Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
The Emergence of Self-Evolving AI
As enterprise cloud platforms scale to serve millions of concurrent users, tightly coupled microservices introduce cascading failure modes that no static runbook or threshold alert can anticipate. During high-velocity events like a Black Friday flash sale, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) face an unforgiving reality: diagnose noisy distributed telemetry in seconds, or suffer cascading outages costing millions of dollars per minute.
While generative AI copilots have accelerated code authoring and log summarization,
AI agents struggle to reliably remediate live production outages
. An on-call engineer battling connection pool starvation does not need an AI agent offering troubleshooting tips or unverified pull requests that might not fix the root cause; they need a governed,
self-evolving AI system
that can:
Diagnose
distributed root causes across cache and database tiers in real time,
Self-patch
by synthesizing, verifying, and mounting executable mitigation tools into live server middleware on the fly,
Self-critique
by computing the marginal credit of every action to separate effective fixes from harmful reflexes,
Remember
by distilling cryptographically signed operational invariants into semantic memory to reduce the chance of identical failures recurring, and
Re-architect
by dynamically rewiring its own multi-agent hierarchy in memory with human sign-off to absorb future surges.
This paradigm is
Self-Evolving AI.
In this Google Cloud research reference architecture, codenamed
Project Chrysalis
, we demonstrate how three foundational research breakthroughs combine into a unified, production-grade architecture that can run on Gemini platform and the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Across simulated Black Friday cache-stampede outages, this governed architecture cut time-to-first-mitigation from 15 to 45 minutes down to 1.8 seconds, reduced HTTP 5xx error rates from 72.7% to 80.0% down to 0.0%, dropped P99 latency from 519.8 ms to 18.2 ms, and evaluated 400 counterfactual traffic policies in BigQuery in ~0.5 ms.
Crucially, this self-evolving architecture does not operate as an unconstrained "black box". To ensure the agent remains secure, reliable, aligned, and contained against rogue behavior, every autonomous action is cryptographically bounded by Google Cloud's defense-in-depth security stack:
Model Armor
to sanitize incoming telemetry against prompt injections and data leaks;
Google Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS)
and Binary Authorization middleware to cryptographically sign synthesized patches and block unverified code from mounting; Open Policy Agent (OPA) Policy Controller to enforce strict SLA guardrails that prevent self-inflicted outages; and Dual-Custody Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) governance to require explicit SRE sign-off before any permanent changes are made to the agent hierarchy.
1. The Incident: The Black Friday Cache Stampede & Why Agents Must Self-Evolve
To see why static playbooks and advisory copilots fail under pressure, consider a classic distributed failure cascade:
The Ingress Surge:
A flash promotion drives a sudden burst of concurrent checkout requests across cold inventory keys.
The Cache Eviction:
Google Cloud Memorystore
(Redis) evicts cold keys under strict Least Recently Used (LRU) memory limits, collapsing the cache hit ratio to zero.
Connection Pool Starvation:
Uncached traffic cascades directly into
Google Cloud SQL
. Once the PostgreSQL connection pool saturates, incoming queries queue past timeout thresholds and the service begins failing with widespread HTTP 500 errors.
The Fatal "3:00 AM Panic Reflex":
Under operational stress, both human responders and naive LLMs instinctively try to
restart the database connection pool
. In a live stampede, dropping connections locks the database kernel, spikes tail latency nearly tenfold, and drives error rates toward total outage.
How a Self-Evolving Agent Adapts Over Time
Conventional AI agents are frozen at deployment with fixed system prompts and pre-registered tools. When a novel infrastructure bottleneck strikes, a self-evolving AI architecture extends those baseline capabilities by synthesizing situation-specific mitigation tools at runtime, scoring the telemetry impact of every intervention, and codifying verified guardrails for future incidents.
For true autonomous resilience,
the agent itself must evolve based on empirical evidence of what worked and what failed
:
Autonomous Self-Patching (Tool Synthesis):
When the agent diagnoses that database starvation is driven by an unthrottled ingress surge and realizes it lacks a built-in traffic-shaping tool, it
writes its own middleware patch
on the fly (an in-memory token-bucket rate limiter), validates its Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), signs it with Cloud KMS, and hot-mounts it directly into the API Gateway.
Causal Self-Critique (Evaluating What Worked vs. What Failed):
After stabilizing the outage, the agent evaluates the telemetry delta of every action taken during the incident. It mathematically penalizes the database restart reflex because it worsened latency, while rewarding its synthesized rate limiter for eliminating server errors.
Cognitive Memory & Organizational Self-Rewiring:
To reduce the likelihood of a repeat outage, the agent writes a signed operational principle into vector memory that blocks database restarts during cache stampedes. It then modifies
its own multi-agent topology in RAM
, commissioning a permanent
Traffic Shaping Specialist Agent
under the supervisor agent so future surges are shaped before they reach the database.
2. The Three Research Pillars of Self-Evolving AI
Self-evolving cloud agents are an active area of applied research focused on resolving the
SRE Trilemma
(balancing exploration safety, structural adaptability, and multi-step credit assignment) by unifying three research pillars on Google Cloud:
1.Serverless Counterfactual Simulation (
Dream-RSI
):
Challenge:
Testing unvetted rate-limiting parameters in live production risks throttling legitimate revenue or re-triggering outages.
Mechanism:
Production request traces are exported to
Google BigQuery
, where the engine replays hundreds of candidate token-bucket configurations in sub-millisecond vectorized memory sweeps to identify Pareto-optimal policies offline.
2. Tri-Level Co-Evolution (
APEX
):
Challenge:
Single-layer prompt tuning provides fragile band-aids, while unconstrained code self-modification risks system instability.
Mechanism:
Agent evolution is separated into three governed timescales:
Layer 1 (Ephemeral Hotpatching):
Synthesizes and mounts in-memory middleware tools to halt active outages in seconds.
Layer 2 (Principle Distillation):
Encodes
Cloud KMS
-signed lessons into
Agent Platform Vector Search
so contraindicated actions are blocked on future alerts.
Layer 3 (Topology Rewiring):
Commissions permanent specialist sub-agents into the active multi-agent Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
3. Step-Level Shapley Attribution (
AgentEvolver
):
Challenge:
During chaotic incidents, multiple interventions occur in sequence; coarse outcome rewards cannot isolate which step healed the service and which caused collateral damage.
Mechanism:
AgentEvolver computes marginal Shapley credit across each execution span using pre- and post-intervention telemetry deltas (P99 latency, HTTP 5xx rate, and database pool saturation), isolating beneficial patches from erroneous ones.
3. The 4-Phase Reference Walkthrough: Self-Evolution in Action
We
implemented this architecture
as an interactive application on Gemini platform. The diagram above illustrates the closed-loop workflow across the
Production Target Service
,
Agent Development Kit (ADK) Multi-Agent Plane
,
Self-Evolution Engine
, and
Defense-in-Depth Governance Pipeline
.
Each phase of the interactive demonstration showcases a distinct stage of the agent's self-evolution:
Phase 1: Ingress Outage & SRE Baseline
What Happens:
Following a 5-request warm baseline, a 50-request concurrent flash-sale surge hits 15 cold inventory keys.
System Impact:
Memorystore hit ratio drops from
100% to 0.0%
, the Cloud SQL connection pool hits
100% saturation
(2/2 active connections locked), P99 latency spikes to
312.8 to 519.8 ms
, and HTTP 500 errors jump to
72.7% to 80.0%
(40 failed checkouts).
Phase 2: ADK Fast-Loop Triage & Governed APEX Layer 1 Hotpatch
What Happens:
Telemetry alerts wake the
Agent Development Kit (ADK)
Supervisor Router Agent
powered by
Gemini 4 Argon
, after
Model Armor
inspects the incoming alert payload to block prompt injections.
Autonomous Self-Patching:
Diagnosing pool exhaustion, the
APEX Layer 1 Hotpatch Synthesizer
generates an in-memory token-bucket rate limiter (10-token capacity, 40.0 req/s replenishment). Before mounting into the API Gateway middleware, the patch passes three automated governance gates:
AST Sandbox Visitor
verifies that forbidden system modules and dynamic execution sinks are absent.
OPA Policy Controller
confirms the replenishment rate meets the enterprise minimum SLA (>= 10.0 req/s).
Cloud KMS & Binary Authorization
signs the artifact digest (EC_SIGN_P256_SHA256) and verifies key provenance at the middleware boundary.
System Impact:
Across a second 50-request surge,
HTTP 500 errors drop to 0.0%
,
Cloud SQL pool saturation drops from 100% to 0%
,
P99 latency recovers to 18.2 ms
, and excess burst traffic is cleanly shed via HTTP 429 (40 requests throttled, 10 served from warm cache).
Phase 3: AgentEvolver Attribution & Tier-2 HITL In-Memory Topology Rewiring
What Happens:
The
AgentEvolver Credit Attribution Engine
audits the incident execution spans, penalizing the database restart reflex ( after spiking latency to 3,800 ms) and rewarding the token-bucket middleware patch (
+0.97 credit
).
Principle Distillation:
The
APEX Layer 2 Principle Distiller
signs and indexes an immutable operational rule into
Gemini Platform Vector Search
:
"Cache eviction stampede: database restart contraindicated; apply token-bucket load shedding."
Tier-2 Dual-Custody Approval:
Rather than relying on temporary hotpatches, the system proposes a Tier-2 structural update: commissioning a permanent
Traffic Shaping Specialist Agent
. Execution pauses in the UI and presents a
Dual-Custody SRE Approval Modal
requiring explicit sign-off from the on-call SRE.
In-Memory ADK Graph Rewiring:
In production cloud runtimes (Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run), container images are immutable; rewriting source files on disk during a live outage violates container integrity and requires disruptive restarts. Instead, once issued a cryptographic human-approval token, the
APEX Layer 3 Cloud Topology Adapter
executes an
in-memory Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) update:
Instantiates the
Traffic Shaping Specialist Agent
in RAM with dedicated rate-limiting, queue-depth inspection, and token-replenishment tools.
Appends the specialist agent directly to the
Supervisor Router Agent's
active sub-agent graph as a parallel peer alongside the
Diagnostic Agent
(leaving the diagnostic node unmodified).
Updates the supervisor's routing instructions and re-binds the live
Google ADK Runner
in memory with
zero downtime and zero container restarts
.
Phase 4: Google BigQuery Counterfactual Replay & Curiosity Chaos Verification
What Happens:
Incident request traces flow into
Google BigQuery
, where the
BigQuery Counterfactual Replay Engine
executes
400 counterfactual policy simulations
across token capacities and replenishment rates.
Sub-Millisecond Discovery & Chaos Proof:
Vectorized in-memory trace replay completes all
400 sweeps in ~0.5 milliseconds
, identifying the Pareto-optimal policy (5-token capacity, 5.0 req/s rate, zero 5xx errors). Finally, the
Curiosity Chaos Red-Team Agent
stress-tests the evolved system in an isolated shadow sandbox by purging 100% of the cache and firing 200 concurrent requests. The newly wired
Traffic Shaping Specialist Agent
absorbs the surge with
0 HTTP 500 errors
and
13% max DB load
, certifying the architecture as resilient.

items.title: Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec API Gateway now supports real-time streaming—including Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, gRPC,
items.content:
Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec
- Google Developers Blog
Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec
OCT. 22, 2026
Mak Ahmad
Product Manager
Geir Sjurseth
Product Manager
Jeremy Whitlock
Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
For most of the last decade, an API call looked like a transaction. A client sent a request, waited, and got a complete response back in one piece. That model is exactly what most API management tooling — including API Gateway — was built to handle, and it still describes a huge amount of production traffic.
But that no longer describes all traffic types. A model generating a response emits tokens as it produces them, not in one batch at the end. An agent working through a multi-step task reports progress as it goes. A dashboard, a collaborative editor, a live inference endpoint — these all need a connection that stays open and carries data in both directions.
Until now, developers building those experiences in API Gateway had to make an uncomfortable choice: put API Gateway in front of their APIs and give up streaming, or route streaming endpoints around the gateway and give up the authentication, API key enforcement, and observability that made the gateway essential in the first place. Teams ended up with a split estate — governed APIs on one path, ungoverned streaming traffic on another.
We're announcing that streaming support in API Gateway is available in Public Preview.
Your streaming endpoints can now sit behind the same gateway, with the same policies, as everything else you serve.
For AI applications, streaming also strengthens API Gateway's connection to Gemini platform. A gateway that uses model routing now streams responses from Gemini, Claude and OpenAI gpt-oss models in model garden in Gemini platform as they're generated, and streaming backends you host anywhere else work the same way. Alongside Apigee and Agent Gateway in Gemini platform, API Gateway is the lightweight entry point to Google Cloud's AI gateway capabilities.
What you can stream
API Gateway now supports the full range of streaming patterns modern APIs rely on:
Server-Sent Events (SSE)
— the de facto standard for streaming model output to a browser or client SDK, and the transport behind most OpenAI-compatible chat completion APIs.
Chunked transfer encoding and HTTP response streaming
— including newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) and any other progressively-delivered response body. Responses are passed through as your backend produces them rather than buffered and delivered at the end.
WebSockets
— full-duplex connections for chat, collaboration, live dashboards, notifications, and interactive sessions.
gRPC streaming
— server-side streaming and bidirectional streaming, so you can put a gateway in front of gRPC services that were previously impossible to proxy.
Streams can stay open for up to one hour. As with any long-lived connection, clients should implement reconnection logic so that a session survives the end of a stream — a well-behaved WebSocket or SSE client should be doing this anyway.
Your API contract doesn't change
This is the part we are most pleased with:
there is nothing new to learn.
Streaming is not a different product, a different resource type, or a different way of describing your API. There are no new extensions to add, no streaming-specific annotations, no separate spec for streaming operations. The same document that describes your existing API describes your streaming API.
Everything you already rely on continues to work exactly as before:
API key enforcement
JWT validation, including Firebase, Auth0, Okta, and Google ID tokens
Service account authentication to backends
Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring integration
Path templating and request routing
During Public Preview, you opt-in when creating the gateway:
gcloud api-gateway gateways create GATEWAY_ID \
--api=API_ID \
--api-config=CONFIG_ID \
--location=REGION \
--enable-streaming
Plain text
Copied
That single flag is the entire difference. At GA, it is planned that streaming will simply be how API Gateway behaves, with no opt-in required and, as during Preview, no changes to your API config.
A hostname you can predict
Alongside streaming, gateways get a deterministic default hostname:
GATEWAY_ID-PROJECT_NUMBER.REGION.gateway.dev
(Example: streaming-test-12345.us-central1.gateway.dev)
Plain text
Copied
Previously the default
gateway.dev
hostname included a generated hash, which meant you could not know your gateway's URL until after you had created it. That is a small thing that causes a lot of friction: you can't write the endpoint into a client config, a Terraform module, a CI pipeline, a firewall allowlist, or a partner integration doc until the resource exists — and if you tear the environment down and rebuild it, the URL changes underneath you.
Now the hostname is a pure function of values you already chose. You can generate it, template it, document it, and commit it to source control before the gateway exists, and you get the same URL every time you rebuild the same gateway in the same project and region. For anyone managing environments as code, or promoting a configuration from dev to staging to prod, this removes an entire category of bootstrapping problem.
Why this matters for AI workloads
Streaming isn't a niche feature for AI applications — it's the expected interaction pattern.
Users expect to see a model's response appear as it's generated, not after a thirty-second pause. Agents need to report intermediate steps. Tool-calling protocols and remote MCP servers depend on long-lived, incrementally-delivered connections. An API management layer that can't stream severely limits the user experience of AI applications.
With streaming, API Gateway becomes a viable front door for that agentic traffic — and the value of a front door is exactly the same as it's always been, only more urgent. AI endpoints are expensive, they consume quota, they need per-consumer authentication and rate limiting, and they need to be observable. These are the governance problems that an AI gateway is intended to solve. The alternative — every team standing up its own proxy in front of its own model endpoint — is how organizations end up unable to answer basic questions about who is calling what.
Model routing
in API Gateway lets you expose a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint and dispatch requests to Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI gpt-oss models based on the model field in the request payload. Model routing plus streaming means clients get a familiar, standards-based streaming interface, while you retain centralized control over which models are reachable, by whom, and under what policy.
Streaming, model routing and
MCP support
are all features within API Gateway that provide a lightweight on-ramp to AI gateway capabilities within Google Cloud. These AI gateway capabilities allow teams to monitor, secure and control agentic traffic of tools, models and agents in their ecosystem, and they're delivered as a composable suite so you can choose the right gateway for each use case. For more expansive AI policies and full lifecycle management, use
Apigee
. To manage and secure agent connectivity, use
Agent Gateway
in Gemini platform. You can also combine these gateways: API Gateway or Apigee can sit in front of your agents and APIs, or behind Agent Gateway so your agents can reach models, tools, and MCP servers. For example, you can route your agent's egress through Agent Gateway for strict security governance, and then pass the request to API Gateway to handle model routing.
What to know during Public Preview
A few things to plan around while the feature is in Preview:
Streaming is enabled at gateway creation time.
Existing gateways can't be converted in place; create a new gateway with the flag to try it.
A few API Gateway features are not available at the initial Preview launch, but will be coming during the Preview time period.
Custom domains via Serverless NEGs and an external Application Load Balancer
Streaming enablement via the Cloud console
Terraform
Latency metrics reflect stream duration.
Request latency for a streaming connection measures the life of the stream, not time-to-first-byte, so expect long-lived connections to change the shape of your latency graphs.
Get started
If you're already using API Gateway, the fastest way to see this working is to point a new streaming-enabled gateway at an existing backend that emits SSE and watch the events arrive incrementally. No spec changes needed.

items.content:
Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond
- Google Developers Blog
Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond
OCT. 21, 2026
Pier Paolo Ippolito
Product Manager
Elia Secchi
Solutions Specialist
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
End to end walkthrough of the new Agents CLI Extension System, with a worked LangChain example and a custom deploy policy
Introduction
When we launched
Agents CLI
at Google Cloud Next '26, we built it around one strong opinion: going from an idea to a production agent on Google Cloud should take a single unified command surface. For teams building with Agent Development Kit (ADK), that opinionated path has worked. You run
agents-cli create
, write the agent logic, and ship to Cloud Run with observability and evals wired up, in about thirty minutes.
The agent framework landscape has grown more diverse in the months since. In addition to ADK, developers today pick between
LangChain
and
LangGraph
, specialized newcomers like
Deep Agents
, or in-house frameworks tailored to a specific business domain. Different teams prefer different frameworks, and the right choice for a greenfield prototype is rarely the right choice for a production migration. Enterprise admins may also have governance policies they want to enforce across the ADLC for all of their development teams, such as: a compliance scan, an SSO gate, a Model Risk Management hop.
Can a team benefit from the deployment, evaluation, and observability work in Agents CLI without being forced to adopt ADK, or without being forced to accept the default behavior of every command? Starting with version 1.5.0, the answer is yes.
Agents CLI now ships with an
Extension System
that lets developers override or add commands without forking the tool.
Version 1.8.0 ships the first-party LangChain extension, which replaces the framework-coupled commands with their LangChain equivalents and leaves the rest of the lifecycle untouched.
We will walk through two journeys below. First, to show you the ADLC with LangChain agents, we'll show you how you can scaffold, run, deploy, and evaluate a LangChain agent through the Agents CLI lifecycle using the first-party extension. Then we build our own small extension that wraps the
deploy
command with a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) scan, demonstrating the pattern enterprise platform teams can use to enforce their own policies across every project. Both journeys use the same mechanism.
The Framework Lock-in Problem
Most agent development toolchains available today share a limitation: they are opinionated about one specific framework, and the surrounding capabilities (deployment targets, CI/CD pipelines, evaluation harnesses, observability wiring) assume the developer has adopted that framework. When your framework matches the tool's assumption, the opinionated path works. When it does not, you're left with three bad options.
The first is to fork the CLI, maintaining a divergent copy and re-syncing it on every upstream release. You pay a permanent maintenance tax, and every upstream improvement has to be hand-merged into the fork. The second is to wrap the CLI behind custom scripts, building a parallel command surface that invokes the underlying tool. The problem is that developers (and their coding assistants) forget about the wrapper and call the underlying tool directly, bypassing the intended abstraction. The third is to walk away and build everything from scratch, which can consume several engineer-months of work that the team had not planned for, and which rarely produces tooling as polished as the upstream project.
The problem shows up in two scenarios. One is enterprise customers adopting Agents CLI: in regulated industries, a central platform team often requires that every
deploy
invocation be wrapped with a compliance check, that
login
route through corporate single sign-on, or that evaluations flow through a Model Risk Management pipeline. Each of these requirements, implemented today, means either forking the CLI or building a wrapper layer. The other is teams that use ADK most of the time but need to run a non-ADK framework on a specific project. Within the Agents CLI command surface, six commands assume the ADK runtime:
playground
,
run
, and four
eval
subcommands. The other eighteen or so (
scaffold
,
infra
,
deploy
,
publish
,
login
, and friends) are framework-agnostic. Without extensions, choosing a non-ADK framework for a single project meant losing access to all twenty-four.
The Extension System handles both with one mechanism.
What are Agents CLI Extensions?
An Agents CLI extension is a directory in a Git repository that contains a single file called
agents-cli-extension.yaml
. The file declares which built-in commands the extension overrides and which new commands it adds. From the
official documentation
:
Extensions are how you adapt agents-cli to a workflow it doesn't ship with — a different agent framework, an org's deploy policy, or a command of your own — without forking the tool.
Extensions take two shapes, described in the
Using Extensions
page. A command override replaces the behavior of a built-in like
playground
,
deploy
, or
eval generate
. The overridden command receives the user's arguments verbatim, so the user experience stays consistent with the native command. A new command exposes a workflow the CLI does not currently provide as
agents-cli <your-command>
. Both shapes can coexist in the same extension, and most non-trivial extensions use a combination of the two.
Extensions are distributed through Git repositories rather than through a dedicated package registry. The design draws from the extension model used by the
gemini-cli
project. There is no central index to publish to, no package format to maintain, and no ownership roster to apply for. Any directory inside any Git repository can serve as an extension, and Git handles the versioning, pinning, and distribution. For enterprise platform teams, this means creating an internal
platform-extensions
repository and pointing their developers at it, with no external registry to coordinate with.
Reference Forms
An extension can be referenced in several ways, depending on where it lives and how the developer wants to use it:
# First-party shorthand, which resolves to the google/agents-cli repository
agents-cli extension add <name>
# Any organization or repository on GitHub, including self-hosted Git servers
agents-cli extension add acme/platform-extensions
agents-cli extension add acme/platform-extensions#soc2-deploy
# A local path, which is typically used during extension development
agents-cli extension add local@../my-extension
Plain text
Copied
The
#<name>
syntax lets a single Git repository hold multiple extensions, with the fragment identifier selecting one of them. Enterprise platform repositories often bundle together a family of related extensions (one for
deploy
, one for
login
, one for
scaffold create
) under a single repo with shared ownership and release cadence.
Scopes
Extensions install at two scopes. The default is the project scope, where the extension and its lockfile entry are committed to the project's own repository. Teammates and CI pipelines pick it up on checkout. The alternative is the user scope, enabled via the
--global flag
, where the extension is stored in the user's home configuration directory and applies to every project on the machine. The user scope is the one you reach for when an extension needs to be available before any project exists, such as a framework bootstrap extension that configures
agents-cli create
itself.
When both scopes define the same command, the project scope wins, and
agents-cli info
surfaces the source of each active command. Scoping is deliberately explicit: the Extension System will not silently merge or override extensions, and any conflict surfaces to the developer at install time or in the
extension list
output.
Lockfile and Lifecycle
The Extension System follows the discipline of package managers like
uv
or
npm
: it resolves a Git reference to an exact commit SHA at install time, records the resolved SHA in a lockfile, and uses the lockfile to re-materialize the exact reviewed code on every fresh checkout. The
agents-cli install
command restores the vendored working copy from the pinned SHA without advancing the pin, which guarantees that CI and local development run bit-for-bit identical code. To advance a pin to the latest commit on the tracked reference, the developer runs
agents-cli extension update
, which re-resolves the reference and re-prompts for third-party trust. The complete lifecycle is in the
Using Extensions → Lifecycle
section.
The Extension System is marked experimental in v1.8.0. The manifest schema and the command surface may still change in breaking ways before the system is finalized, so teams depending on it should pin their Agents CLI version.
Running LangChain Through Agents CLI
The LangChain first-party extension is a project template: one command scaffolds a working LangChain agent wired into the Agents CLI lifecycle. The resulting project has zero
google-adk
dependency and deploys to Cloud Run through the same code path an ADK project uses. The template's own description reads:
Run LangChain agents, LangGraph graphs, and Deep Agents through the agents-cli lifecycle.
In modern LangChain (version 1.0 and later), the state management layer is provided by LangGraph, so the three frameworks share a common graph representation. The template serves all three communities with the same code.
Prerequisites
Before we begin, we need:
Python 3.11 or later
uv package manager
Google Cloud SDK (gcloud)
Python
Copied
A Google Cloud project with billing enabled is also required. If you do not have one yet, it can be created at
console.cloud.google.com
.
If Agents CLI is not already installed on the development machine, it can be installed in a single command:
uvx google-agents-cli setup
Python
Copied
Finally, we authenticate with Google Cloud and enable the APIs the agent will depend on at runtime:
gcloud auth application-default login
gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT_ID
gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com run.googleapis.com artifactregistry.googleapis.com
Plain text
Copied
Step 1: Scaffolding the Project
Scaffolding and extension installation are the same operation. Rather than installing an extension first and then scaffolding a project, we point
agents-cli create
directly at the extension's template, pinned to a specific release tag:
agents-cli create my-agent \
--agent google/agents-cli/extensions/langchain/template@v1.8.0 \
-d cloud_run
cd my-agent && agents-cli install
Plain text
Copied
The output confirms the scaffold succeeded:
Agents CLI v1.8.0
Fetching remote template: google/agents-cli/extensions/langchain/template@v1.8.0
> Verifying GCP credentials...
> ✓ Connected to project: your-project
✅ Success! Your agent project is ready.
Plain text
Copied
The scaffolded project already contains an
agents-cli-extension.yaml
at its root, which is auto-loaded at project scope the next time any command is invoked. There is nothing to install manually, because the project itself is the extension's installation. A developer scaffolding a LangChain project does not need to know the Extension System exists. The command looks and feels like a native
agents-cli create
invocation that happens to produce a LangChain project instead of an ADK one.
Step 2: Inspecting the Generated Structure
Here's what the scaffolder produced:
my-agent/
├── agents-cli-extension.yaml      # auto-loaded project-scope overrides
├── agents-cli-manifest.yaml       # project configuration (deployment target, etc.)
├── GEMINI.md                      # project's coding-agent guide
├── langgraph.json                 # LangGraph dev-server configuration
├── pyproject.toml                 # langchain, langgraph, langchain-google-genai
├── Dockerfile                     # identical CMD to any ADK project
├── app/
│   ├── agent.py                   # exports root_agent: CompiledStateGraph
│   ├── fast_api_app.py            # exposes `app: FastAPI` on A2A
│   └── app_utils/
│       ├── a2a.py                 # LangGraphAgentExecutor and A2A routes
│       └── telemetry.py           # Cloud Trace and GenAI logging
├── scripts/
│   ├── run.py                     # drop-in replacement for `agents-cli run`
│   ├── eval_generate.py           # drop-in replacement for `agents-cli eval generate`
│   └── publish.py                 # Agent-Runtime-aware refusal wrapper
├── tests/
│   └── eval/datasets/basic-dataset.json
├── deployment/                    # Terraform infrastructure modules
├── uv.lock
└── .agents/skills/agents-cli-langchain/   # the project's own coding-agent skill
Plain text
Copied
The structure looks similar to an ADK project: same
app/
, same
tests/
, same Terraform under
deployment/
, same manifest at the root. The two differences are the
agents-cli-extension.yaml
at the top (which carries the LangChain overrides) and the
langgraph.json
file (which configures the LangGraph dev server used by the local playground).
The main agent definition lives in
app/agent.py
:
"""LangChain agent: a Gemini ReAct agent with a sample tool."""
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain.agents import create_agent
